analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "We'll hear arguments first this morning in 76-15-72, United States against Grayson. Mr. Solicitor General, you may proceed whenever you're ready. Mr. Chief Justice, may it please the Court. This case presents the issue whether a United States District Judge, in imposing a sentence upon a convicted defendant, may take into account as one of the factors his belief that the defendant lied under oath at the trial. The jurisdiction of this Court is pursuant to 28 U.S.C. Section 1254, subsection 1, and writ of certiorari to the Third Circuit. The facts are not in substantial dispute. The respondent, Ted Grayson, was under confinement in the federal prison camp at Allenwood, Pennsylvania, since August 29, 1975, under a three-year sentence for distributing a controlled substance. This is a minimum security facility and is guarded only by offense. On October 11, 1975, Mr. Grayson absented himself from the facility, and there's no dispute about this fact. He was apprehended two days later by agents of the Federal Bureau of Investigation in a New York City apartment where he initially denied his identity but subsequently acknowledged it. He was indicted by a grand jury in November 1975, a month later, was tried in February 1976, and was convicted by a jury on February 6, 1976. The jury obviously rejected his defense that he left under duress because of threats by another inmate, one Alex Sarge Barnes, to whom he claimed he was indebted to the extent of 40 cartons of cigarettes arising out of poker game losses. On March 12, 1976, the sentencing judge imposed a sentence of two years consecutive to the sentence that the respondent was then serving. And the judge stated expressly that the reasons for his sentence were to deter respondent and others from similar conduct. And secondly, and I quote, it is my view that your defense was a complete fabrication without the slightest merit whatsoever. A motion for new trial was denied, an appeal was duly noticed, and a panel of the Third Circuit affirmed the conviction without opinion. Upon rehearing, the panel reconsidered the case and, in a split decision, vacated the sentence and remanded the case for resentencing, finding that the trial judge's consideration of the respondents lying on the stand was in conflict with one of its decisions, a case called Poteet v. Falver, and that, for this reason, the sentence was tainted and couldn't stand. The judge concurring in the initial opinion for vacating the sentence added the constitutional reasons that the holding or a contrary holding would penalize the right of a defendant to take the stand, would deter other defendants from testifying, and impose punishment for perjury, a separate or independent defense. The dissenting opinion distinguished the Poteet case, which was thought to govern, pointing out that in Poteet, after a jury conviction, the trial judge endeavored to cause both convicted defendants to confess their guilt. One of them did and received a particular sentence. The other persisted in his claim of innocence despite the jury's contrary verdict. And the judge in the state court thereupon pronounced a considerably more severe sentence. And this dissenting opinion in our case properly pointed out that the district judge here only sentenced him because of lying on the stand and not for his refusal to confess. The dissent also observed that this was not a sentence for an independent crime, but merely a consideration of the character or behavior of the defendant at the trial. Interestingly enough, the dissenting opinion suggested two limitations on the consideration of a defendant's mendacity at trial. First, that the trial judge should be convinced beyond a reasonable doubt of the lying under oath. And second, that the falsity of the testimony should be necessarily established by the finding of guilt. He had no difficulty with either condition in this case and would have affirmed. It is also interesting that neither of the judges who voted to vacate the sentence had any difficulty with the fact that the testimony was false or that it was necessarily established by the finding of guilt. Or if they did, they certainly did not express it in their filed opinions. This question has been considered by all the circuits and all but the District of Columbia Circuit until this case from the Third Circuit had held that a trial judge may consider the fact that a defendant lied under oath in determining the appropriate sentence. So long, of course, that the sentence does not exceed the permissible limits established by statute. This is consistent with the expression of the Congress. In 18 United States Code, Section 3577, we find the Congressional statement, and I will quote it. It's brief. And this statute is found in that portion of the code that provides for the obtaining of a pre-sentence report. As a sentencing tool available to the district judge who must pronounce sentence. And I emphasize the congressional use of the word conduct of a person convicted. And certainly lying under oath at the trial is an act which might fall under the classification of conduct. And the court, of course, witnesses this himself. And the statement that no limitation should be placed on the information would certainly seem to legitimatize the trial court's action here unless there is some constitutional reason why he may not do it. So we submit that there is no constitutional reason. There, as the dissenting opinion pointed out, is no punishment for a separate or independent offense. The offense of perjury is a separate and independent offense. But it carries a sentence of five years. And this sentence was within the permissible limits for the sentence of escape from confinement. And was not because he, and was not an additional penalty. But merely a consideration of an appropriate sentence as demonstrated by the conduct of the defendant who appeared before the court. Mr. Solicitor General, if the position of the Third Circuit were sustained, would there be a tendency, at least in some cases, for the prosecution to institute a new case, a new indictment for perjury? And if that were so, might not the defendant be worse off than having the judge merely take it into account? Indeed, he might be. Prior conviction for bank robbery. Certainly, the sentencing court could take that into consideration in formulating the sentence for escape. It could take into consideration the fact he had been previously indicted for bank robbery, could it not? Indeed. Even though he had not been convicted? Yes, Your Honor. Or even arrested and not indicted. And in Williams v. New York, this court in 1949, I believe, indicated that the fact of an arrest or indictment could also be taken into consideration as having a tendency to reveal something about the background, character, and conduct of the defendant. It would also be true if the judge hadn't said, given his reasons. That's very true, Your Honor. And this is the trouble that I have with the decision of the Third Circuit. The district judge here, in utter candor, in expressed candor, because he said, I am saying this while I pronounce sentence. So if I am wrong, a reviewing court can't tell me that I am wrong. And if he were denied the right of considering the mendacity of the defendant, he might just say nothing and pronounce the same sentence, and it would not be reviewable by any court, because no one could speculate why he did it. Now, I'm not suggesting that a judge would be dishonest about it if this court should say that he could not consider it. But it would certainly be a temptation not to explicate reasons. And I might observe that the Senate Bill 1437, that's sometimes referred to as the son of S-1, a previous Senate bill that was proposed in an earlier Congress that will amount to a revision of the criminal code, requires the explication of reasons for sentences that depart from presumptive sentences that are to be established by a mechanism set forth in that proposed legislation. And this would mean that a judge, desiring to depart from a presumptive sentence, could not take into consideration the fact that the defendant lied in his presence, under oath, in the courtroom, at a time when he might be expected at least once to have respect for the process of justice. Another contention that we'd like to make is, in many states, juries sentence. In fact, perhaps in as many states as they do not, I should have that number for the court and I can furnish it if the court wishes. If this is indeed a constitutional limitation, if the sentencing agency may not take into consideration the fact that a defendant lied, then a sentencing jury could not take this into consideration either. And we would have the anomalous situation of a jury rejecting a defendant's defense because it found it incredible, beyond a reasonable doubt, and then having to disregard its determination in deciding what disposition to make of the defendant. And we submit that that kind of anomalous situation isn't good constitutional sense or good common sense, and that this decision of the Third Circuit should be reversed. If there are no other questions at this time, with leave of court, I would reserve the balance of my time for a rebuttal. Very well, Mr. Solicitor General. Thank you, Mr. Chief. Mr. Humphrey. Mr. Chief Justice, may I please the court. The 1949 decision of this court in Williams v. New York was a reflection of the concept of individualized sentencing. And that case placed a particular emphasis on the need for a sentencing judge to consider a variety of factors which would relate to a defendant's need for and prospects for rehabilitation. Therefore, the court held that a judge without due process safeguards can consider such characteristics of a defendant as past criminal conduct, even if that conduct had not resolved in a conviction. Justice Black, in that opinion, indicated very clearly that hearsay could be relied upon, did he not? That is correct. Would not the personal observation of a judge in the courtroom be more trustworthy and material than the hearsay information which necessarily comes into a pre-sentence report? The government has contended that this would make the determination by a judge more accurate, the fact that he was there and observed the testimony. We would contest that position for a variety of reasons. First of all, as it pertains to perjury, perjury is an inherently difficult crime to prove. It has historically been subject to the so-called two-witness rule, unlike other crimes. And as this case illustrates, the particular factual situation in this case, we're dealing here with a conflict between the testimony of two convicted felons. The judge happened to choose or happened to believe the testimony of the government inmate witness. But it is our position, and I will discuss this in just a moment, that, in fact, the jury's determination of guilt in this case was not at all inconsistent with the defendant's testimony. What if, hypothetically, the pre-sentence report showed that of 20 or more persons interviewed by the probation officer, a dozen of them said that this man was unreliable, untrustworthy, and known to be a man who constantly dealt in falsehoods? Could the sentencing judge take that into account? Your Honor, I believe that he could. Under Williams. Under Williams, and even under our position in this case, because that presumably would be conduct which was a reflection of the defendant's character generally outside of the unique pressures of a criminal trial. And we think that this is a crucial difference in this case. Just what do you mean by the unique pressures in the context of your sentence, as you've stated to choose? A man who has been convicted of a serious criminal offense, it would not be surprising that this type of man would generally lie in an attempt to avoid the hardships of incarceration. We think that a criminal trial itself places a unique pressure on a defendant. Well, one of the pressures it places on him is that he takes an oath to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, isn't it? Yeah, that is correct, Your Honor. Well, do you think that cuts in your favor? No, we're not excusing perjury. We're not attempting to say it's okay for a defendant to commit perjury. Perjury can be punished. A defendant who commits perjury on a stand can be charged and convicted of perjury. Well, then I'll put to you the question I put to the solicitor. Do you think it's, is it in the interest of your client to have the government be required by this court to prosecute him separately for the perjury? Indeed, I think it's in the interest of all defendants that the government be required to charge and to try a defendant who they suspect a perjury. We would have no argument. That would be the only way, or at least it would be one way to discourage perjury other than giving heavier sentences, wouldn't it? That is correct. And at least a defendant. Would you suggest that would be good for defendants generally? I would say that Mr. Grayson would much have preferred to have been charged and be given the opportunity to persuade a jury that he did not get convicted of perjury, rather than have a judge make a summary determination and impose an additional increment of sentence without any due process safeguards whatsoever. I find it difficult to square that with the idea that you concede that the court may take into account the hearsay statements of a dozen people outside that he's a liar. Well, again, those kind of statements go to a defendant's character outside of the context of the criminal trial. Well, yes, but what if the probation officer interviews the defendant after conviction, which would be a normal procedure? And he writes down this report. I talked to him and asked him all sorts of questions, and he continually lied to me. I just couldn't get anything out of him. He just lied to me. And he writes it in his probation report. And the prisoner knows as well as anybody that that pre-sentence report is going to the judge. Could the judge consider that report? I believe he could, Your Honor. Well, that isn't outside the context of a criminal trial. He, as a matter of fact, is awfully close to immediately preceding the sentence. Well, it is not in the trial situation. And in that particular case, one of the problems we have with a judge considering perjury is that it tends to chill the right of a defendant to testify on his own behalf. Well, what you're saying is that the court in sentencing can take into consideration the fact that the defendant has lied on other occasions, but on the one occasion he took an oath to tell the truth, it can't take into consideration the fact that he thought he lied. That is right, because there are, and for several reasons, one, that a defendant is under unique pressure in a criminal trial. Two, that the consideration of the judge of that factor, by the judge of that factor, tends to chill the right of other defendants to take the stand and testify, even to get truthful testimony. How is any other defendant going to get any less pressure? I'm very interested. You know, he's under more pressure than anybody else. This particular response? No, any defendant is no more in trouble with perjury than any other witness. That is correct, but if... Now, if he could testify without taking an oath, he'd be in pretty good shape. That's correct. Like he used to do in Georgia. That is right. And that they do, apparently, under the Continental System still. No, in the Continental System, they have to find out how he was not guilty because he starts out guilty. So let's don't get into that. Here's my problem. If, along with my brother White's question, if the pre-sentence report says that this man was arrested for perjury, could the judge add two years on that? Yes. And the difference between that and this is what? The difference is, well, if the pre-sentence report says he was arrested for perjury in some other proceeding, then that would not, the judge could consider that. And he committed perjury while being tried for another offense. Yes, I believe the judge could consider that. And the difference? And the difference is that in this particular case, the defendant, in choosing whether or not to take the stand, if the court upholds the government's position here, a defendant will be chilled in his choice of taking the stand. Yeah, he could be chilled in committing perjury. Is that bad? No. If he's persuaded not to commit perjury, is that bad? Well, of course it's not bad. Is that bad? If that's the purpose of the sentence, then I think it's an improper sentence because... Well, do you think that this man will again deliberately commit perjury at a trial? Well, we would contest that he committed perjury in the first place. Well, do you think he will commit it again? Well, do you think he'll think about it the next time? Well, of course I'm sure that he'll think about it the next time. But if that's the purpose of the sentence, then it indicates that the judge was sentencing him for the purpose of deterring him from committing perjury. Which is what the judge said he was sentencing to deter him from escaping. Well, he said that one of the reasons for his sentence was deterrence. But if the reason we're sentencing is to deter defendants from committing perjury, then we are in fact sentencing them for the substantive crime of perjury. Well, I don't know where you get we. I'm not in this. I'm not sentencing him. You want to sentence him? You go ahead. If a judge were to sentence him on that basis, then... Well, you agreed that he could if the pre-sentence report said, remember, judge, when he was being tried before you last month, he committed perjury. And, indeed, he was indicted for it. Not convicted. He was indicted for it. He was charged with it. The judge could take that into consideration. Well, I would say that, yes, if it was not in the context of this criminal proceeding before the judge. But it was a similar one the week before. If it was the week before, yes. If it was not this particular criminal proceeding. I see. Now, all you want is that in this particular proceeding, because this man is subject to perjury, he cannot be considered for sentencing. Well, that's one of the reasons. I think that there is a temptation for a judge to sentence him or to increase the increment of sentence because of suspected perjury because he wants to either punish the individual for falsely testifying in his court or because he wants to deter other defendants from doing so. And that... And he can't do it for you to leave? No, I don't believe he can't because that would, in effect, be a sentence for the substantive crime of perjury without having been charged or convicted. Well, when he raises it, because the pre-sentence report says that this man was arrested for murder three years ago in... uh... Guam. Can the judge consider that in the sentence? Yes, he can. Williams would say that he can. Well, how can he punish him for that murder in Guam? He's not punishing. In that case... Well, what's the difference? Why is it not punishment there? Okay. There are four recognized purposes of sentencing. Protection of society, deterrence, punishment of the individual, and rehabilitation. The government has contended in its brief, and the eight courts of appeals which has decided this issue in favor of the government's position, all reject the concept that this is a punishment or a sentence imposed for deterrence and that it's for rehabilitation. Similarly, a consideration of a murder in Guam three years ago, or the charge that he murdered, would be relevant only to the question of that defendant's need for and prospect for rehabilitation. You can't punish him for that. Well, I question whether, at least I would agree with that characterization. I would think that many a trial judge who is sitting as a sentencing judge and reads, as my brother Marshall has indicated, in the pre-sentence report that the man was convicted for, or indicted for murder in Guam, charges dismissed three years ago, indicted for an armed bank robbery two years ago, charges dismissed, increases the sentence not in the hope of rehabilitating the man for these things, since most sentencing judges don't even mention the fact, but simply because he figures this man is a bad apple, and he's a worse apple than the conviction for this particular offense indicates. Well, I think that that is the same thing that I'm talking about. If he's looking at the character of the individual, and he says, as a result of the fact that this guy is a bad apple, as shown by his murder three years ago, then he should be incarcerated for a longer period of time, because it would take a longer period of time to rehabilitate him, or he can't be rehabilitated, and therefore we've got to keep him in. And Williams, when it talks about these various kinds of sentencing factors, talks in terms of rehabilitation. You look at the character of the man, you can't punish him for a crime that he hasn't been convicted of. Well, Williams wasn't dealing with rehabilitation because the decision based on the hearsay evidence, the hearsay material in the probation report, led to his electrocution, so there was no rehabilitation. Well, it was a lack of rehabilitation, lack of possibility of rehabilitation, perhaps. Going back to Mr. Justice White's question, the setting that he suggested, you referred to the unique pressures under which a defendant suffers when he's on trial. After the conviction, I suppose those pressures haven't gone away, have they? After the conviction and before the sentence. Well, perhaps he's still under some pressure, yes. I was talking about the trial situation and the... Yes, but what if the sentencing day comes and the judge wants to know from the defendant if he has anything to say given his right of allocution? And he allocutes. He talks at great length and the judge says, well, you're just lying. And in his sentence, he says, I think you've lied right here before me. Of course, you weren't under oath, but you were lying. And he says, I'm going to increase the sentence for that reason. Would that be permissible? That's a closer case. One, because he's not under oath and therefore apparently would not be subject to a perjury conviction. However, I would take the... But the pressures must be there. I would take the position that in that particular case, the judge should not consider it because, again, it would chill the right of a defendant to allocute. And the... First of all, perjury, I don't think is that relevant to the question of rehabilitation because of the fact that... That it's not... And the fact that he's under oath or not isn't that relevant to whether the judge should be able to take it into account, is it? Well... It's the fact that he's a... That he's a congenital liar that the judge takes into account, whether it's under oath or not. I think that, you know, that the judge can take into account the fact that a man is dishonest. But in this particular context, in trial, for the variety of reasons, the chilling effect upon his right to testify, the fact that the unique pressures that the defendant is under, I don't think that he should consider this. We're not saying that that it's going to go unpunished. He can be punished for it. But in this particular context, it is improper. What if a judge, like Judge Muir in this case, had said there is in the pre-sentence report a good deal of information that is hearsay saying this man constantly spreads malicious rumors about his neighbors. This is maybe an undesirable characteristic, but it doesn't influence me in sentencing. Nonetheless, when he exercised his right of allocution, as Mr. Justice White's hypothesis, he lied before me. And I regard this as a frustration of the judicial process, which I am going to take into consideration and add to the sentence. Would you think the judge couldn't do that? Well, it depends. If he's doing it for the purpose of punishing this man for doing what he's doing or telling the judge falsehoods, or if he's doing it for the purpose of deterring that individual or other individuals from doing likewise, I don't think it's proper because he was not charged and convicted of that, of any crime, and to punish him or to attempt to deter others from that conduct without the charge and conviction, I don't think is proper. However, if he says that is a reflection of the man's character and his needs for and prospects for rehabilitation, it's a close case. As I said, the fact that he's not under oath may distinguish it from the case that we have at Barr here because he would not be subject to other punishment after a charge and conviction. Do you know whether the new proposed new criminal code touches on this question? Well, the new proposed criminal code in the very first section of it sets forth the reasons for sentences. Section 101, subsection B says... Does it require a statement of reasons? Yes, it does. Yes. Furthermore, it states in section 101 B4 that one of the purposes of sentencing is to promote the correction and rehabilitation of persons who engage in such conduct, recognizing that imprisonment is generally not an appropriate means of promoting correction and rehabilitation. The whole concept of individualized sentencing has undergone quite a reevaluation in recent years. But it doesn't forbid taking into consideration the character of a defendant? Well, no. In fact, specifically, it has a section there very similar to the statute 3577, which would permit them, but then it says really rehabilitation is not a goal that is being served by incarceration of a defendant. I wanted to point out at this time something about the facts of this case just to illustrate the problems created by this practice. Here's a defendant who denies that he committed perjury and we have a jury verdict which was not inconsistent with his testimony despite the contentions of the government and the statements of the dissenting judge in the court below. The defendant testified that he was being pressured by an inmate because of this gambling debt that he left because he's afraid of getting killed and he went to his apartment, his legal residence in New York City and was apprehended by the FBI a couple of days later. The judge, in charging the jury on this defense of duress and coercion stated that there must be no reasonable opportunity for the defendant to have avoided the compulsion without committing the crime and charge a jury that they must apply a reasonable man's standard. Therefore, it's obvious that the jury could have said this man was under duress, he did feel that his life was in danger but a reasonable man would not have taken the action he took. A reasonable man would have gone to the authorities at the Al-Alan prison camp and asked for their protection. Mr. Humphrey, would you make the same basic argument you make in this case if the jury verdict were inconsistent with the defendant's testimony? I would make the same basic argument in a constitutional, on the constitutional point. I think that this case can be decided without reaching the constitutional question. I believe that the court could, if the court recognizes the difficulties which this particular practice creates, I think the court can exercise its supervisory powers over the federal courts and impose, for example, those... Mr. Humphrey, supposing we had a case in which a defendant had not taken the witness stand and the trial judge before sentencing said to his lawyer, you know, I'd heard this witness on the... heard this man on the witness stand, I might have decided the case differently on the merits and the lawyer had said, well, he couldn't take the stand because to deny the charge he would have had to tell the truth. I mean, telling the truth would have hurt him. He didn't want to lie so he stayed off the witness stand. Could the judge take into consideration in sentencing him that this man had been sufficiently interested in veracity not to take the stand and try to defend himself falsely? I suppose that the judge could take that into consideration. I've never seen any case where that has been discussed or whatever, but I... I'm sure it happens quite often, aren't you? Don't you think there are a lot of defendants who don't take the stand because they just don't want to lie? Well, there may be an appreciable number. I would say that they don't represent the majority. I was in court yesterday for arguments and Mr. Justice Marshall indicated that it was ordinary or usual for a defendant to misremember events. And I think that is the usual thing. When we're dealing with men who have committed serious crimes, lying to avoid incarceration is not something that is unusual. You're making a presumption that everybody who's tried is guilty or something. No, I'm certainly not. One of the points in our argument is that those not guilty will be dissuaded perhaps from taking the stand and testifying on their own behalf because of this very practice. If an individual knows that he's got a close case and he knows that all the judge has to do is disbelieve him and he's going to get twice the sentence that he would normally get, that's going to weigh heavy on the minds of an appreciable number of innocent defendants. You mean an innocent defendant will not take witness to him? That's right. I believe that there is pressure even without, if we leave this issue aside, there's pressure on an innocent defendant to plead guilty because of the plea bargaining system. If he can get a sure six months, rather... But please don't bring plea bargaining in this case. We have enough problems in there. But the point I'm trying to make is that that pressure exists already and when you throw this into the pot for consideration, not only is he going to get a... The judge is required to ignore the fact that this man has deliberately lied to him. Just ignore that. That's right. It's all hard to do. That's true. It's hard to do and that is one of the problems. There's a tremendous temptation. Well, the problem is two-sided. You don't seem to recognize other problems. Part of the problem is that one way of stopping all this is not to lie on the witness thing. That's correct. That's one way of stopping it. That is certainly correct and as I've stated, an individual is subject to punishment for that. We're not saying it's okay. But when a judge, again, does it because he wants to punish that man or he wants to deter others and he is in fact sentencing him for the subsequent crime of perjury? Just like he sent him for the crime of murder in Guam. Yes, and I believe that that is an improper. That's all right. No. That was all right. Only if it reflects upon his character and need for rehabilitation. I thought you said that in this very case, if the Supreme Senate report said this man was arrested for murder in Guam three years ago, the judge could consider that. That's right. But I stated that he could not consider it if he was imposing sentence for punishment or to deter other murderers. My question is, in this very case, if the judge had said, quote, the pre-sentence report shows that you were arrested for murder in Guam three years ago and I am taking that into consideration in this sentence, that that is perfectly all right. It is all right, as I stated, if it relates to his character. No, no, don't add anything to it. In this very case, it would be all right or not. Your Honor, I have to add a qualification. It's not all right generally. It's not all right if he's punishing him for that. Obviously, he could be arrested for murder in Guam while testifying in the United States. So, I mean, that's true. Right, but it's not this, it's not... He can consider everything except perjury. Yes, it is not this judge's, but it is not this judge's function to punish for other criminal conduct. He, only when that criminal conduct reflects upon this man's character and need for or prospects for rehabilitation. Mr. Humphrey, you were court appointed by the district court? That's right, Your Honor. By Judge Muir himself? That's right. And you had been his clerk? That's right. Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Humphrey. Do you have any further, Mr. Solicitor General? Mr. Chief Justice, with the leave of court, I would waive the balance of... I have a couple of questions, Mr. Solicitor General. Yes, sir. There is, as I'm sure you would concede, an absolute constitutional right to plead not guilty to any criminal charge. I would do. There is also an absolute constitutional right to, for a defendant to take the witness stand in his own defense in any criminal trial. That's my understanding, too.
